slides.title: It starts with you.
slides.text: You are an {identity}: something that can own things and decide. More exactly, you are a {human} identity. You never sign anything yourself; you act through the agents you own.
slides.deep: An identity's ID is the hash of its birth record, typed by its kind, so it outlives every key. Every identity keeps a signed history of its policies and keys. Identity types: human, coop, agent.

slides.title: Your phone is your agent.
slides.text: Your phone runs an {agent}: an identity that acts on your behalf. Inside it sits a {signer}: a {key}, a secret only the phone holds, that can say “this really comes from this agent.” The agent belongs to you: you are its {owner}, and it owns nothing itself.
slides.deep: An agent identity is owned by exactly one human or coop. Its signer is just its current key; how the key is kept is up to the device it runs on: derived from the passkey's PRF plus a salt on a phone, the keychain on a laptop, an environment variable, secret manager or HSM on a server.

spec.summary: An agent is an identity owned by exactly one human or coop. Its record says who it is; what it may do comes only from policies (D58).

records.name: theos/identity@1 (an agent)
records.about: The agent's own history: one record per change of key or epoch, each signed by the agent's current signer.
fields: agent:b3: and the hash of the agent's birth record (D50)
the current signing key; on phones derived from the passkey's PRF plus a salt
the agent's own lock; envelopes are sealed to it (D57)
signer revision: +1 on every key rotation
the hash of the next signer's public key (pre-rotation)
continuity epoch: +1 on every restore or reinstall
the signer's running number within this epoch (D61)
by the signer of the rev it names

records.name: theos/epoch@1
records.about: Written once by a restored or reinstalled device before anything else.
fields: the agent's last records it still has

rules.text: Every agent has exactly one owner, a human or a coop, fixed at birth; an agent is never in a role.
An agent's rights are exactly the live policies whose to is the agent and whose on is its owner; owning gives nothing.
A record with rev r+1 is valid only if its signer hashes to the next of the record that set rev r.
An epoch record raises epoch by exactly one; within an epoch, seq starts at 1 and rises by one per record.
A record is identified by (agent, epoch, seq); two different records with the same triple prove the signer lied (D61).
The agent's Loro peer ID for a piece of data is the first 8 bytes of b3("theos/loro-peer" ‖ agent ID ‖ epoch ‖ data ID), so a restore never reuses an op ID (D63).

slides.title: You and your first agent are born together.
slides.text: When you start, your phone's agent makes its signer and signs one record: your birth, its own birth, and its first {policy}, a signed statement of what an agent may do: “this agent may act for you.” From then on, you exist, and you own it. Nothing has to come first.
slides.deep: One genesis record creates the human and its first agent together: no chicken-and-egg. It commits to the agent's next key in advance (KERI-style pre-rotation). Both IDs are its hash, typed once as human and once as agent (D50); a record can't contain its own hash, so inside it the two are “this human” and “this agent”.

spec.summary: One record creates a human (or coop) and its first agent, and gives that agent its first policy.

records.name: theos/genesis@1 (identity)
fields: pre-rotation: hash of the next signer
to “this agent”, on “this human”; operations act, own, govern
by the new agent; key = agent.signer

rules.text: For a birth record g without its signature, the human ID is human:b3:b3("human" ‖ cbor(g)) and the agent ID is agent:b3:b3("agent" ‖ cbor(g)).
Inside a birth record, “this human” and “this agent” name what the record creates; a record never contains its own hash.
sig.by is the created agent's ID and sig.key equals agent.signer.
The first agent starts at rev 0, epoch 1, seq 1; the birth record is its seq 1.

slides.title: Each agent gets only what you give it.
slides.text: You can have many agents: your laptop, your watch, a server, even an AI assistant. Each gets its own policy from you, saying what it may do for you. Your phone may do everything; your watch only what concerns your health; your assistant only your shopping list. What an agent may not touch, it gets no keys for either.
slides.deep: An agent has two parts. Who it is: its own identity, owned by exactly one human or coop, with its own signer. What it may do: only what policies from the identity it acts for say, here act for you on your health data. Owning an agent gives it nothing. The same policy decides which keys it gets (Keys chapter, D57, D58).

spec.summary: Every further agent gets one policy from the identity it acts for, with conditions on act.

records.name: theos/policy@1 (on an identity)
fields: the identity the agent acts for: its owner
keyed by name: act, own, govern (D56)
only these data operations, keyed by name
identity policies don't expire unless they say so (D50)
from the identity's birth record to the signing agent

rules.text: An agent policy is valid only if signed by an agent of on whose own policy includes govern.
Its operations and conditions are within the signing agent's own (D59).
An agent may do an operation on data only if its policy on its owner covers it and the owner's roles and policies on the data cover it (D58).

slides.title: A new device joins with a one-time code.
slides.text: To add your laptop, your phone writes an {invite}: a one-time key, an expiry, and exactly what the new device may do. You scan its code with the laptop, which makes its own signer and signs its birth together with the one-time key. The invite already says what it gets, so no other device of yours has to be online, and the code is worthless after one use or ten minutes.
slides.deep: The laptop's birth record names the invite and carries a second signature by the one-time key; together they are its policy, exactly as granted. Two births citing one invite are both invalid. An invite can't grant more than the agent that signed it holds (D69).

spec.summary: Pairing without a second device online: the invite is the policy, signed in advance; the birth record proves possession of the one-time secret.

records.name: theos/invite@1
records.about: Written into the identity's history by an agent with govern.
fields: the identity the new agent will act for
one-time key; its secret travels only out of band (QR code or typed code)
exactly what the new agent gets (D56, act conditions D58)
by an agent of on with govern

records.name: theos/genesis@1 (agent by invite)
fields: the new agent's own, made on the new device
by invite.key over the record without both signatures

rules.text: An invite is valid only if signed by an agent whose policy on invite.on includes govern, and its grants are within that agent's own operations and conditions.
A birth by invite is valid iff invite_sig verifies under invite.key, the invite is in its after, and its signed time is before invite.expires.
A valid birth by invite gives the new agent exactly invite.grants on invite.on, as a policy of invite.on; it ends like any policy (D58, D60).
If two different births cite the same invite, both are invalid.
The owner may end an unused invite with an ending; a birth that didn't see the ending loses (D60).
The one-time secret never travels over theOS; only the device that scanned or typed it can sign invite_sig.

slides.title: You and Mia start a home.
slides.text: Together you form a {coop}: an identity made of identities. It has a {role}, a named set of identities, called “members”, which holds you and Mia. A policy lets that role act for the coop. Neither of you is the coop alone, and it lives on even if one of you loses every agent.
slides.deep: There are no membership records: a coop's members are simply its “members” role, and policies say what that role may do. A role holds humans or coops, never agents or signers.

slides.title: A coop decides by its own policies.
slides.text: A policy on the coop says what its “members” role may do for it: act, ordinary changes for the coop, and own, writing and ending the policies on the coop's data. The third kind, govern, changing the coop's own roles and policies, goes to a {governor}: a role with exactly one identity, for now you. One top, so nobody can remove each other at the same moment. Before you step down, you hand govern on.
slides.deep: Same shape as every policy. The members role gets act and own, one signature each (1 of 1, D49). Govern goes only to the governor role, which holds exactly one identity (D59). Below the top, if two members undo each other at the same moment, both stand and the governor repairs. Counts like 2 of 3 come later as condition plugins.

slides.title: Coops can hold coops.
slides.text: Your street is a coop of homes, and a home is a coop of people. The street's “members” role holds the home coops, and a policy on the street says what they may do for it: here, act, but not own or govern. A home acts through its own members' agents. Coops can sit inside coops as deep as you like, never in a circle.
slides.deep: The street's members role lists home coops; this policy gives that role act on the street, and the street's governor keeps govern. An agent of yours acts for the street through the chain: your agent's policy on you, the home's policy for its members role, the street's policy for its members role. Roles are checked whenever they change; loops of coops are settled when the view is built (D63).

slides.title: Losing your phone.
slides.text: Your phone is gone. From another of your agents, you revoke the lost phone's policy, and from then on it can do nothing for you. What it could still read, and which keys turn, comes in the Keys chapter.
flow: revoke the phone's policy from another agent
turn the keys it could open
the phone acts for no one
slides.deep: Pre-rotation belongs to agents: each agent's history commits to the hash of its next signer, so a leaked key can be replaced. Revoking an agent's policy is an ending like any other (Endings chapter).

slides.title: Identity, in short.
list: Humans and coops are identities that own and decide.
Agents act for exactly one owner, each with its own signer, and only by its policies.
A role is a named set of identities; a coop's members are its “members” role.
A coop's members act and own; one governor governs, for now.
Policies say what a role or an agent may do for an identity: act, own, govern.
slides.deep: Three identity types: human, coop, agent. Ownership points from humans and coops to agents and data; authority to act flows back only through policies.
